facts.claim: SQLite’s documentation: on one desktop PC, finding “linux” in 517,430 Enron emails took about 22.5 seconds by reading every email, and about 0.03 seconds through its full-text index.
Apache Lucene’s documentation: its index of words is an inverted index, because for each word it can list the documents that contain it.

Spärck Jones (1972), testing three collections of documents, argued that a match on a rarer word should count for more than a match on a common one, and found this very simple weighting gave considerable gains.
Robertson and Zaragoza (2009) call BM25 one of the most successful text-search methods to come out of their probability-based theory of ranking.

Apache Lucene’s documentation (version 10.5.2): its BM25 scoring sets how fast repeats stop helping (k1) to 1.2 and how much a long page counts against it (b) to 0.75 unless told otherwise, as this search box does.
Porter (1980): his stemmer, cutting word endings by rule, turned a list of 10,000 different words into 6,370 stems, about a third fewer.
BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021) tested ten search systems on 18 public datasets and found BM25 a reliable yardstick on data the systems were not trained for.
scikit-learn’s guide: precision is the share of what was picked that is right; recall is the share of the right ones that were found.
